title: Man charged after Grangetown fire in which woman and niece died
description: A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder following a fatal house fire in which a woman and her seven-year-old niece died.Natalie McDonald, 34, d
body: A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder following a fatal house fire in which a woman and her seven-year-old niece died.Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August, along with Valentina Foster.Jaden Wright has been charged with two counts of murder as well as multiple grievous bodily harm offences, Cleveland Police said.Wright, of no fixed address, will appear at Teesside Magistrates' Court later.Senior investigating officer Katie Smith from Northumbria Police said: "This has been a truly tragic incident, and my thoughts remain with the families of all those involved."I would like to thank local residents for their support and patience during this complex investigation."Anyone with information has been asked to contact Cleveland Police.Katie Nicolson from Crown Prosecution Service North East said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with Cleveland Police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court."We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial. "It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

schema.headline: Man charged after Grangetown fire in which woman and niece died

title: Russian strike hits rail workers in new deadly attacks on Kyiv
description: At least 12 people have been killed and 20 injured, including two children, in overnight Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukraine's capital Kyiv a
body: At least 12 people have been killed and 20 injured, including two children, in overnight Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukraine's capital Kyiv and the wider region, officials say.In Kyiv, six of the eight casualties were railway workers of the state Ukrzaliznytsia company after a depot was hit. Fires were reported in three city districts. Four people were killed in the town of Boryspil where a residential building was hit.Russia's military said its "massive strike using high-precision weapons" targeted Ukraine's "military-industrial and fuel-energy" facilities.One person was also killed in Ukrainian strikes on Russia's western Belgorod region, acting Governor Aleksandr Shuvaev said.Separately, a drone attack hit a major Russian Baltic Sea port in Ust-Luga, triggering a fire, Leningrad regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.Ukraine says targets like Ust-Luga - which handles millions of tons of petroleum products each year - are legitimate as they help finance Moscow's war effort.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday morning that nearly 350 rescue workers had been working through the night in Kyiv and the surrounding region after the latest strikes.In a post on social media, he said Russia had fired a "significant number of jet drones and ballistic missiles". Eight other Ukrainian regions were attacked, Zelensky said, adding that an Indian national was among the casualties.Ukraine's Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivsky later said the Indian man - who turned 26 on Tuesday - was killed in Boryspil. The latest attacks come after 38 people were killed in Russian strikes on a weapons depot in the Kyiv region on Friday, causing shells, mines and drones to detonate.On Monday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged Putin to end the war, saying every day of conflict set humanity back. India's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow.

schema.headline: Russian strike hits rail workers in new deadly attacks on Kyiv

title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
description: Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that ha
body: Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.The jury found him guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996.Dressed in a black suit, the 63-year-old stood impassively in the Las Vegas court as the verdict was read, before saying he would appeal. During the trial, the court heard a recording of a police interview in 2008 in which Davis said he was in the car from which shots were fired, but did not himself fire the bullets that killed Shakur.Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.As the verdict was read out on Monday, Shakur's relatives held hands, some hugging and crying.Shakur was 25 when he was slain at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now. Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money. In closing arguments, his lawyer Michael Sanft urged the jury to discredit his client as a liar who just told tales to sell books. "There's no proof," he told the jury. But within hours of the jury being handed the case on Monday, they reached a guilty verdict. Just before the court emptied out, Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny set Davis' sentencing for 13 October.While reading out some procedural steps in the case, Davis appeared to interrupt by raising his hand."I would like my stuff," he told the judge, mentioning some personal items including his phone.He continued: "I would like to appeal this matter." The judge explained that this could happen after sentencing.

schema.headline: Duane "Keffe D" Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Kemi gets Tories battle ready' and 'Posh makes some dosh'
description: A number of the papers look forward to Andy Burnham's first parliamentary appearance as prime minister.The Guardian, external says his statement to MP
body: A number of the papers look forward to Andy Burnham's first parliamentary appearance as prime minister.The Guardian, external says his statement to MPs will "drive home" his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control. The paper has spoken to a Downing Street source who says Burnham's statement will be all about proving that he can "bring back hope". The Sun, external says this marks the end of the prime minister's "honeymoon", and says now he will have to deliver on Britain's real problems of "welfare, a flatlining economy" and defence.Some hints on the government's plans for that last issue are in the Times, external where the Chancellor, John Healey, says he will set out a "clear path" to spending 3% of national income on defence in the Spring. But he warns that will mean "difficult" decisions in the Budget this autumn.Kemi Badenoch's shake-up of her Conservative shadow cabinet over the Bank Holiday weekend is hailed as a "ruthless reshuffle" by the Daily Mail, external, which says she is getting the Tories "ready for battle" amid rumours of an early election. The Financial Times, external believes Badenoch's first goal should be to restore the Conservatives to their "traditional position" as the country's "major right wing party".The Daily Express, external highlights a report backed by the former defence minister, Al Carns, which urges the government to drop its Northern Ireland Troubles Bill over fears it could trap soldiers in "endless legal jeopardy". Carns is quoted as warning that "justice is not served when the process itself becomes the punishment". Ministers say the existing Legacy Act protects terrorists and leaves veterans exposed, while their plans will fix a "broken system".The Daily Mirror, external says Ghislaine Maxwell is preparing to "beg" US President Donald Trump for her "freedom". The paper believes it is her "last hope" to end the 20-year prison sentence she is currently serving for procuring girls for Jeffrey Epstein.Cancer patients receiving immunotherapy could survive for twice as long if they received their treatment in the morning rather than the afternoon, according to research picked up by the Daily Telegraph, external. It says doctors at The Christie hospital in Manchester found it made the biggest difference for people with skin and lung cancer.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Kemi gets Tories battle ready' and 'Posh makes some dosh'

title: Feeling nostalgic for summer? How to beat the back-to-work blues
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByKate WhannelBusiness reporter and Nick TriggleHealth correspondentThe alarm wakes you with a shock, the summer holiday is
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByKate WhannelBusiness reporter and Nick TriggleHealth correspondentThe alarm wakes you with a shock, the summer holiday is over and it's time to face that inbox full of unread emails.This time last week, life was very different. You enjoyed late nights, lazy mornings balancing family fun and you time.Even if you enjoy your job, the transition from holiday to work can be hard, particularly in September as the days begin to shorten. Here are some ways of making the transition a little bit easier. Tick off small tasksIt can be tempting to launch straight into tackling the hardest task first.But careers coach Sarah Robinson says it's better to "ease back in" by starting with small, manageable tasks and "quick wins". "It's about trying to build momentum, because I think sometimes it can just feel overwhelming when you've got a massive inbox," she says.Counsellor Susan Carr agrees. She says it isn't possible in every industry but where viable "be a bit kinder with your expectations of what you need to do on that first day back in the office."That could mean spending the day going through emails rather than a full day of back-to-back meetings.Tara Humphrey, a primary care leadership consultant, advocates keeping her out-of-office on for her first day back."It's about hiding, if you can, just to give yourself that bit of headspace."She also says re-entry into work life can be made easier by a clearly-written out-of-office message, encouraging people to follow up when she is back in the office - that eases the stress of whether you have missed something important while on holiday. There is an alternative. She recalls a colleague who would simply delete all the emails he had been sent during his holiday. "He said, 'if people want me, they'll come back to me'."Stay touristy - but at homeCarr says it is also worth remembering what was enjoyable on holiday and "whether there's a way of integrating that more into your everyday life".While it may not be realistic to have a siesta every day, you could try cooking some Spanish food, she suggested. She also recommends holding on to the curiosity we have when in a new place and trying to be a tourist in our own area. "If we go away somewhere else... we might be looking at the architecture, visiting buildings, and I think - and I know I'm guilty of this in Manchester - we don't always appreciate what's on our doorstep."Psychotherapist Dr Joy Conlon, who runs wellbeing coaching service Alive 365, agrees."Bring one restorative part of the holiday home with you. This might be an evening walk, eating without looking at a screen, reading before bed instead of being on a screen or just spending more time outdoors. Reflect on your roleRather than treating the symptoms, it may be worth looking at the root cause of the back-to-work blues.Before, she was a counsellor, Carr worked as a solicitor. "I was vaguely aware before I went on holiday that things weren't right and I was quite stressed," she says."I went away on holiday and then I came back and suddenly I was in floods of tears every day. It wasn't just a case of needing time to adjust, it was a sign I needed a rethink."But how can you tell between a temporary nostalgia for long lie-ins and genuine unhappiness with your job?"It probably sounds really obvious," Carr says, "but I suppose one of the signs of that is how long it goes on for.""It's that length of time but also maybe the intensity of the feelings."Lying on a sunbed, it can be easy to fantasise about quitting everything and retraining as a scuba diver instructor or yoga teacher, but Carr warns against a "knee-jerk reaction". "It's about taking time and reflecting on how you might go about making a change."Book your next holiday – and make it activeIt is not just the holiday itself that makes them so enjoyable and beneficial, the anticipation of going also plays a key role, says Dr Mark Williamson, chief executive officer of Action for Happiness, a charity.And what type of holiday or how long you go for can make a difference to the overall impact.Williamson points to what he says is "genuinely surprising" research , externalwhich suggests physically active holidays may be better for wellbeing than simply lying by the pool."If you include some walking, cycling, swimming, exploring you're more likely to get back feeling refreshed," he adds.Another factor to consider is the length of your next break, he says. "Longer breaks give a bigger boost, but it seems to fade faster, partly because you return to a bigger mountain. "There's some evidence that shorter but more regular breaks bring more wellbeing benefits. The refresh from five days away may feel not far off ten, but you can do it twice as often."Get in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Feeling nostalgic for summer? How to beat the back-to-work blues

title: I climbed the career ladder and got my dream job at 30 - then I hit burnout
description: Image source, TCOLS StudioImage caption, Jo said she felt like someone had flipped a switch in her brainByGemma DunstanBBC WalesUpdated 3 hours agoJo
body: Image source, TCOLS StudioImage caption, Jo said she felt like someone had flipped a switch in her brainByGemma DunstanBBC WalesUpdated 3 hours agoJo Hooper spent her 20s trying to climb the career ladder, quickly rising through the ranks with promotions and pay rises."I loved being good at it," said Jo, a former communications professional.But just after she landed her dream role at 30, Jo struggled with burnout and had to take time off work.Burnout, external is recognised by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a state of physical and emotional exhaustion.Recent statistics show 22 million working days, external were lost in Britain because of work-related stress in 2024-25.Jo, now 39 and based in Penarth in the Vale of Glamorgan, said: "I wanted to be a head of communications by the time I was 30, which I did by doing all things you'd expect, working long hours, saying yes to everything including mad things like taking my boss's kids to school."Figure caption, I'm on a mission to convince people to work less"I genuinely thought these were all good opportunities, and I was going to grab them with both hands," said Jo."I remember being in the bathroom crying, hyperventilating, but I never thought 'this isn't sustainable', never thought 'I can't do this any more'."I just thought I needed to change job and I'd be fine. I thought the fix was being in a different organisation but the way I behaved, what I thought was expected of me, was the same everywhere."Jo hit burnout a year into her management role, and it led to two breakdowns within a year."I definitely think it was a case of being forced to stop by my body and mind," she said."I found it really difficult to make decisions, like my brain was working slower. I remember feeling like someone had flipped a switch and my brain had just broken."Image source, Jo HooperImage caption, Jo said during her burnout she could barely sleep and felt sick when brushing her teethImage caption, Dr Jill Williams works with those struggling from burnout after her own experience She said: "It's actually perfectionists or those who go the extra mile who are more likely to experience this."The same traits that get you promoted will be the same ones that burn you out, unfortunately."Public Health Wales' Amy Davies said the phrase burnout could be used interchangeably for stress, but said the two were different things."Stress can feel like drowning, but burnout can feel like having nothing left to swim with," she said.Both experts have helped BBC News bust burnout myths and misconceptions."It's not necessarily just work, we can see it an awful lot in carers and students, any situation where there is long-term stress," said Williams.As it is caused by prolonged, unmanaged stress, it can stem from any persistent, demanding role or responsibility.Is burnout different from depression or anxiety?Burnout and depression are distinct conditions, and the WHO does not consider burnout to be a mental health condition or illness."If burnout experiences are unaddressed it may lead to those conditions developing," said Davies.Will a holiday fix burnout?"Sometimes it can be helpful, but it also needs to come with changes to the context that's causing the distress," said Davies."For many people rest is necessary, but it's not always enough. If you go back to work and your attitude to work is the same, then you're going to have the same result, so something needs to change," added Williams.Jo ended up leaving her career after she realised it was not sustainable. She was diagnosed with anxiety and depression."I've learnt the hard way that rest doesn't fix burnout, and it certainly didn't fix the breakdown for me. Actually changing the things that burnt you out or broke you down is the only way to get over it."Now I'm a woman on a mission to convince others to work less, because I spent 10 years not doing that, and it nearly broke me."Jo does public speaking and coaching to support business owners and employers to help others avoid reaching burnout."I'm in control, I run my business, I get to decide how it works, I get to decide what I do and who I work with, and that's a huge part of the process for me," she said."I detest this optimisation culture of trying to be as productive as possible. Feeling like we constantly have to optimise ourselves and productivity is just forcing us into working more and living less... I think it just needs to get in the bin."Image caption, Trade union leader Laura Doel said stress is the number one risk at work for union workersSome workforces have raised concerns about staff members leaving jobs due to burnout, including midwifery and teaching.Hannah Leonard, from the Royal College of Midwives union, said: "Midwives do an extraordinary job, and they deserve to feel pride in their profession, not burnt out within a few years of qualifying".Neil Butler from the teaching union NASUWT said: "Changes must be made to bring back the joy into teaching. While it is a relentless grind we will continue to lose good teachers from classrooms in Wales."Laura Doel from Trade Union Congress Cymru, said: "Our research shows that stress is the number one risk at work, higher than traditional dangers like exposure to chemicals, working at height and unsafe machinery."She said actions by employers who offer wellbeing measures are welcomed, but tackling the root cause of stress such as "low pay, insecure contract and impossible workloads" was key.A spokesperson for the Health and Safety Executive, Britain's national regulator for workplace health and safety, said: "Employers have a legal duty to protect workers from risk factors that cause work-related stress by assessing and properly managing key areas of the work."The Welsh government said it was working with employers and trade unions to reduce pressures, support staff wellbeing and ensure appropriate mental health support was available.If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: I climbed the career ladder and got my dream job at 30 - then I hit burnout

title: Shein shares fall in long-awaited stock market debut
description: Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell in their highly anticipated stock market debut on Tuesday as the firm listed in Hong Kong after a long quest t
body: Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell in their highly anticipated stock market debut on Tuesday as the firm listed in Hong Kong after a long quest to go public.It comes after failed attempts to list in the US and UK, as concerns were raised over issues including Shein's labour practices and its environmental impact.Once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn (£74bn), Shein is now valued at around a quarter of that figure, as the firm faces other challenges like heated competition and trade tensions.Shein became hugely popular, especially among younger people, due to its ability to source the very latest fashions at ultra-low prices through a vast network of factories in China.At a ceremony to celebrate the listing, chief financial officer Leigh Gui said the company's model of selling large numbers of small orders with rapid payment options now reaches about 160 markets worldwide."Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion," he said after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading.On Monday, Shein priced its shares at HK$48.56 each, raising ‌13.6 billion Hong Kong dollars ($1.7bn; £1.3bn) from the listing.That gave the company a stock market valuation of $26.3bn.Shein's shares fell by as much as 10% in early trading before the losses eased. At lunchtime, they were around 3.5% lower at just under 47 Hong Kong dollars each. The disappointing debut suggests the market is not convinced that Shein's growth can make a "comeback", said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.Shein has more than 273 million active customers who placed a total of more than a billion orders in the year to the end of March 2026, the firm said in a filing ahead of the listing.But Shein now faces higher costs, regulatory scrutiny and more competition, while investors are increasingly drawn towards technology companies, Chanana said.For customers, the slump in Shein's shares is a sign that the firm's cheap prices are "becoming harder to sustain", which may lead to higher prices, she added.Shein was founded in China in 2008 and is now headquartered in Singapore.The firm's long road to the stock market highlights the geopolitical pressures and regulatory scrutiny faced by Chinese companies with global ambitions.The company once looked set for one of the largest stock market debuts ever by a Chinese firm, with Wall Street in its sights.Its business had surged during the Covid-19 pandemic as people, stuck at home, turned to online retailers.Shoppers shared clips of themselves trying on large numbers of its garments, a trend called Shein Hauls, boosting the company's online presence.An initial public offering (IPO) in the US - by far Shein's largest market - would have offered it a chance to further increase its global profile and tap into Western financing.But the firm faced resistance from US lawmakers, who objected to the planned listing over concerns of forced labour in Shein's factories. In response to such allegations, the company has said it takes a "zero-tolerance policy for forced labour".It has also been accused of copying other designers' ideas. Shein has said "it takes all claims of infringement seriously" and that it respects the rights of all designers.Shein also explored the possibility of making its stock market debut in London but faced similar opposition.The BBC has contacted Shein for further comment.Its rivals are feeling the pressure too. In August, Temu-owner PDD reported lower-than-expected quarterly revenue.Shein is also being investigated by US and European regulators over its business practices.The company also needs to find ways to stand out from its rivals, that are now also using predictive technology to make their websites more appealing to shoppers, said Jason Hsu from Rayliant Global Advisors."Shein is not longer a unique player," Hsu said.Despite these challenges some analysts still see strong potential for Shein.Investors will be scrutinising whether the company can navigate these issues, such as shifting logistics out of China to avoid the US and EU's import fees, Deglise-Favre said.The slump in the firm's valuation shows "genuine deterioration", but it is still backed by a "formidable supply chain" and a global reach, she added.People are still buying the company's goods, but costs have weighed on its business and have shown that its business model does not generate profits in the way it once did, said Dudarenok.As a listed company, Shein will need to "prove its margins still work in a world of tighter regulation, tariffs and more expensive customer acquisition," she added.

schema.headline: Shein shares fall in long-awaited stock market debut

title: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy
description: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it loo
body: The video lasts only seconds.A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The timestamp on the CCTV footage reads 10:59:53 local time.What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery from before and after the disaster have begun to reveal the scale of the destruction. Much of the border complex appears to have been swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.Gyirong was one of the places devastated by the floods that tore through the region on 26 August.Just across the frontier, at Rasuwagadhi in Nepal's Rasuwa district, the destruction was also extensive. The Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China was swept away, along with Nepal's immigration and customs facilities. Timure, the small trading settlement clustered around the crossing, was devastated."This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet. The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders," says Ajay Dixit, a Kathmandu-based hydrologist.The route remains an important gateway between Nepal and China. It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.Nepal's Department of Immigration has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 8:35:03am local time (10:52am Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.Tika Ram Pokharel, a senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, was the only member of his office known to have survived. He had travelled to Kathmandu to sit an exam that day.But he says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area."Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel told the BBC.Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.At 8:37am - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day."My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Reuters: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network."Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck."But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy

title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of peopleByLyse DoucetChief international correspondentReporting fromTorkham crossing and KabulThe elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind."It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins."But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.The expulsions show no sign of stopping. Image source, AFPImage caption, Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR."In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan."We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all."I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry."We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says. "But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law". Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".Image caption, Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children. Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified."I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house. "We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work."I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country. Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.  But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.Image caption, Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend secondary school and university in Taliban-run AfghanistanAt the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face."There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide. The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition."No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states. As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"He answers his own question: "Nothing."We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense. All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

schema.headline: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban

title: Updated flu vaccine ready as NHS regroups from busiest summer ever
description: Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual, external with the Super-K strain.Super flu is not a medical t
body: Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual, external with the Super-K strain.Super flu is not a medical term, and it does not mean the virus has become harder to treat, just that people are yet to build up immunity against it.Flu vaccines are updated annually to ensure they are a good match for the type of flu circulating. Influenza viruses constantly mutate and experts have to predict these changes ahead of time.This year's vaccine has had a few tweaks, including one to better match subclade K.It is not clear when flu will hit this year, and whether it will be a bad season. But experts often look to southern hemisphere countries, like Australia and New Zealand, to gain a better understanding of how the UK could be affected.Their flu season peaks in July or August. Australia has had fewer cases than last year, external, but New Zealand has seen high numbers, external.Dr Amanda Doyle from NHS England said it was best to be cautious."Last year's flu season came early and was made worse by a new variant, which had a major impact for patients and put enormous pressure on urgent and emergency care services across the country," she said."With the NHS experiencing its busiest summer on record, staff have started preparing for this winter earlier than ever – and with services already under significant pressure, it is vital that everyone offered the vaccine comes forward."Everyone is at risk of catching flu. It does not matter how fit and healthy you are, or your age.Dr Doyle said: "Flu can really knock you for six, and for some children and pregnant women it can mean becoming seriously ill or ending up in hospital."The vaccine cannot give you flu. Instead, it helps your body know how to fight the virus.Children, from the age of two upwards, get a nasal spray version, while adults have an injection. A single dose is all that is needed to offer protection ahead of winter.High Street pharmacies are offering NHS flu vaccines, along with GPs and schools. People who do not qualify for a free jab can pay about £10 to £20 for one.School children and pregnant women can get a free NHS flu vaccine from September onwards. You can get a free one from October if you:are a child aged two or older who has not started school yetare aged 65 or overhave certain long-term health conditionslive in a care homeare the main carer for an older or disabled person, or receive a carer's allowancelive with someone who has a weakened immune systemare experiencing homelessness or staying in a homeless hostel or night shelterMore adults are also being offered another vaccine this winter to protect against RSV or Respiratory Syncytial Virus, which attacks the lungs.From this September, adults will be invited to have the vaccine when they are 65, rather than waiting until 75, if they have certain pre-existing health conditions, such as chronic lung disease.

schema.headline: Updated flu vaccine ready as NHS regroups from busiest summer ever

title: Lionel Messi retires: How Argentina legend's decade of dominance almost never happened
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lionel Messi scored eight goals and registered four assists at the 2026 World CupByAndy CryerBBC Sport Senior
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lionel Messi scored eight goals and registered four assists at the 2026 World CupByAndy CryerBBC Sport Senior Journalist"I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give."Lionel Messi retired from international football on Monday as Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player. He captained them to World Cup glory at Qatar 2022 and to Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024.But the world was almost denied his most successful period in the famous blue and white shirt.On Sunday, 26 June 2016, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, Messi broke the hearts of a nation.Just two days after his 29th birthday and soon after missing a penalty in Argentina's Copa America final loss to Chile in a shootout, Messi decided he had seen enough.After 113 appearances, he was adamant. In his mind, he would never pull on an Argentina shirt again."For me, the national team is over. I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion," he said.The pain was understandable. Argentina had lost in the 2014 World Cup final, plus Copa America finals in 2007, 2015 and now 2016. The player many classed as the world's greatest had failed when it mattered most for him."It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over," Messi said, fighting back tears after another trophy chance slipped away. "I think this is best for everyone."Fortunately for Argentina, Messi would have second thoughts.Over the subsequent 10 years, he completed one of football's greatest ever stories. But it was a decade of dominance that almost never happened.Since that retirement U-turn, Messi has played a further 94 times and scored another 70 goals for Argentina. He has lifted four major trophies.The six-week period between his June 2016 retirement declaration and the 12 August announcement he would play on for the "love of the country" could be considered the most significant in Argentine football history - even in world football.Figure caption, Does Messi have the greatest international career?'He lacks the character to be a leader'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Diego Maradona and Lionel Messi both won one World Cup with ArgentinaAs Messi departs the international stage, words of criticism 10 years ago from the country's other legendary number 10 seem almost laughable."He's a really good person, but he has no personality," Diego Maradona said just weeks before Messi's first retirement. "He lacks the character to be a leader."Back then it was the comparison with Maradona that was held against him. Yet Messi had already won eight La Liga titles and four Champions Leagues with Barcelona and was a five-time Ballon d'Or winner, and not yet 30.Maradona's club career hadn't come close, but Messi's only major international honour had been Olympic gold at the 2008 Games. Maradona had almost single-handedly won the 1986 World Cup for Argentina.It's hard to imagine it now, with Messi shirts dominating the last two World Cups, the Argentina team being built completely around him and the nation's fans worshipping him to an almost religious extent – but, back then, there was a lot of criticism."He's not as good as Diego", "he goes missing on the big occasion", "he is part of the country's failure". All accusations that were thrown in his direction.This wasn't the first time Messi had considered walking away either.Spanish football expert – and Messi biographer – Guillem Balague said: "Leo goes really down when he loses. He felt the pressure of being the captain of Argentina and the Maradona thing."Pecho Frio, people in Argentina called him, which means cold chest. It was an insult to say he had milk in his veins. So when he failed in 2016 at the Copa America, that was the third time – the first time in public – he had decided to leave the national side."The two previous ones was a matter of letting him lick his wounds, but this one he came out and said I've had enough. He sometimes cannot help himself as he says what he thinks."The Maradona versus Messi debate is now surely over. Messi is Argentina's greatest, by most judgements. There are many who will say he is challenging Pele for the title of football's greatest ever.A campaign, a statue and many apologiesFigure caption, Messi becomes men's all-time leading World Cup scorerEven people who criticised Messi eventually said sorry.From the moment Messi quit his country, shockwaves reverberated around Argentina.Yes, he had lost in four successive finals. But he was also the country's record goalscorer and the world's best player.The 'Get Messi back' campaign started immediately as team-mates called for him to change his mind just minutes after his announcement."I can't imagine a national team without Messi," said goalkeeper Sergio Romero.The social hashtag #NoTeVayasMessi (Don't go Messi) was used more than 20,000 times within 24 hours.By that time, Argentina's President Mauricio Macri had already spoken with Messi over the phone to try to convince the Barcelona star to reconsider."I told him not to pay any attention to the comments being made because, in truth, we are very happy" with the job he has done," Macri told journalists at the time.Less than a day later, the mayor of Buenos Aires, Horacio Rodriguez Larreta, had unveiled a statue in Messi's honour and called on the public to show him their love."As a football fan, Leo, I am asking you to please reconsider your decision," the mayor said.Thousands of fans gathered in central Buenos Aires, while street signs throughout the capital displayed implored Messi to play on for Argentina.Maradona stated Messi had to stay to take the team to the 2018 World Cup.'It reminded us how much we loved him'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Messi retires with 125 goals in 207 appearances for ArgentinaEdgardo Bauza became Argentina coach in August 2016, replacing Gerardo Martino after the Copa America failure. He lasted just eight months – but maybe his first few days were his most important.The first thing he did was travel to Barcelona to persuade Messi to change his mind. The huge clamour for Messi to return proved irresistible."I love this country and this shirt too much," Messi said as he returned to the international fold."I'm grateful to all the people who wanted me to continue playing with Argentina. Hopefully we can give them something to cheer about soon."Still, success didn't come instantly. In 2018, Argentina fell to France in the last 16 of the World Cup and many wrote off Messi's chances of ever lifting the trophy.Quite incredibly, Messi did not win a senior international tournament until the age of 34 - and then he went on to win four in barely three years, including the 2022 Finalissima.Questions about his international future were raised after each of those triumphs, but he played on to his sixth World Cup in 2026 where he scored eight goals and registered four assists en route to Argentina's defeat by Spain in the final.He was strolling through games, lacking the speed of years gone by, but somehow proving every bit as effective.The final took place in the same stadium where Messi 'retired' a decade earlier."When Messi retired [10 years ago] it reminded us all how much we loved him," said Argentina fan Benjamin who was in the Metlife for the 2016 showpiece final."When I heard him retire, I cried, the country cried. He did get criticism but only because everyone cared so much. Without Lionel Messi, Argentina would still be waiting for their next World Cup since 1986."Messi's footballing future became a matter of fresh doubt after the death of his father Jorge just three weeks after this year's World Cup final.This decision seems final and, at 39, another return to international football looks unlikely.But South American football writer Tim Vickery said an official farewell in Argentina could be on the cards."Remember that, as a result of their behaviour at the World Cup, the next game Argentina play on home soil will only be in front of a crowd at 50% capacity," Vickery told BBC Radio 5 Live."But once those punishments are out of the way, I'm sure it will be in the mind of the Argentina FA: 'Why don't we hold a game back in Buenos Aires? River Plate, they have the biggest capacity in South America. Why don't we do an official farewell there? What do you think about it, Lionel? One last time?'."Figure caption, Argentina fans thank Lionel Messi

schema.headline: Lionel Messi retires: How Argentina legend's decade of dominance almost never happened

title: US Open 2026 results: Novak Djokovic's tearful exit leaves tennis great's future more uncertain than ever
description: Be warned: Novak Djokovic has made a fool of those who have doubted him before.Some questioned if the Serb would challenge for the sport's top honours
body: Be warned: Novak Djokovic has made a fool of those who have doubted him before.Some questioned if the Serb would challenge for the sport's top honours again after he dropped out of the world's top 20 amid a two-year major title drought in 2018.Djokovic proceeded to win four of the following five Grand Slams, doubling his tally of majors with 12 across the next six years.But three years have now passed since he landed his men's record 24th major title at the US Open.And, as the 39-year-old fought back tears mid-match on Sunday night, this latest loss in New York felt different.Staring at a first opening-round Grand Slam exit since 2006, one of sport's all-time greats simply had nothing left, beaten 7-6 (7-5) 5-7 4-6 6-2 6-1 by Argentina's Navone.For so long now Djokovic has not only defied time, but appeared to be improving with it.That was evident at this year's Wimbledon, where he outlasted Felix Auger-Aliassime, 14 years his junior, in a five-set thriller that became the longest quarter-final in the tournament's history.Even in his late 30s, Djokovic has been the one challenging Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, the new dominant forces in the men's game.At the Australian Open in January, he ended Sinner's bid for a third-straight title in a sensational five-set comeback victory. He then led Alcaraz by a set in the final, before fading to a four-set defeat.After early exits in Paris and New York, there is an inevitable sense that Melbourne was his best chance to secure an outright record 25th major triumph and cap a career unparalleled in every statistical measure.Djokovic was despondent after the match, saying he "despised every moment I spent on the court for that"."When it comes to the match itself, and the overall feeling of how I felt with my body and playing, it was really not enjoyable," Djokovic said."But, from the perspective of the crowd and support, it was incredible."I'm very sorry that I didn't perform as well as I should have, could have, or wanted - for them."The four-time winner's shock first-round US Open defeat means:Djokovic will drop out of the world's top 10 for the first time since July 2018His record streak of 78 successive wins in first-round matches at Grand Slams is overAs is his perfect 37-0 record in the first two rounds at the US OpenHe suffered a first-round exit at a major for the first time in 20 years, when the then 76th-ranked Serb lost at the 2006 Australian OpenDjokovic's refusal to disappear from contention on the sport's biggest stages has prolonged the final embers of the 'Big Three' era that captivated crowds for the best part of two decades.But, for the first time in almost 24 years, the next world ranking update will have a top 10 missing at least one of Djokovic, Rafael Nadal or Roger Federer.Nadal, a 22-time major winner, called time on his career aged 38 in 2024, two years after 20-time slam champion Roger Federer did so aged 41.While Djokovic, who will turn 40 next May, is still going, they all share one thing in common - they each last won a slam aged 36.Ken Rosewall remains the oldest men's singles slam champion in the Open era, winning the 1972 Australian Open two months after turning 37.There is no doubt that the game has become far more physically demanding over the 54 years since.Djokovic prevented Federer from breaking Rosewall's record when he saved two championship points to win the 2019 Wimbledon final, one month before the Swiss turned 38.And early exits are still rare for Djokovic at the Grand Slams. He has reached at least the semi-finals eight times at the past 12 majors.Since winning his last slam, Djokovic achieved his lifelong goal of winning Olympic gold at Paris 2024.With that triumph - two months after knee surgery and three weeks after losing to the Spaniard in the Wimbledon final - Djokovic became only the fifth player to complete the career 'Golden Slam'.Since then, his attention has been on breaking his tie with Margaret Court of 24 major singles titles.He has slimmed down his schedule to prioritise the majors. In 2026 he has contested just seven tournaments - four Grand Slams and three Masters 1000 events - and his 21 Tour-level matches are his fewest in a season since 2004.Reacting to Djokovic's defeat, former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "You can't substitute matchplay. You can't be walking into a Grand Slam on a hot and humid day and expect to get through a five-set match. "I know he's super-human in many ways but it's going to catch up with you."Djokovic has stated his desire to continue in the sport until the next Olympics, in Los Angeles in 2028.It would be a fitting stage for his farewell - not least that it would be exactly a decade since his ability to still compete for the biggest prizes was first questioned.Discussing retirement in his recently released documentary, Djokovic said: 'Why would I talk about retirement when I still keep proving to myself that I can still win?'But, as of Sunday night, legitimate doubt has been cast on whether that remains true.

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Novak Djokovic's tearful exit leaves tennis great's future more uncertain than ever

title: Heaton Park synagogue attack memorial service attended by 800
description: Hundreds remember synagogue attack victimsImage source, Family handoutsImage caption, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, were killed in the attack on t
body: Hundreds remember synagogue attack victimsImage source, Family handoutsImage caption, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, were killed in the attack on the Heaton Park Synagogue in ManchesterByJudith MoritzSpecial correspondentDaniel WittenbergSenior producer and Angela FergusonNorth WestThe Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner were among about 800 people who attended a memorial event for the victims and survivors of last year's Heaton Park synagogue attack.Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed, and three others injured, as they tried to defend their place of worship from attacker Jihad al-Shamie on 2 October 2025.Relatives of the bereaved and some of the survivors were among the speakers at Monday's service of remembrance at the synagogue in Manchester.Prior to the event, Rabbi Daniel Walker said the Jewish community feels less safe now than it did immediately after the attack.He said rising antisemitism, combined with a lack of action to "deal with core problems", had left many members of Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation – and British Jews more widely – feeling increasingly vulnerable.Two seats remained empty for the service, bearing the names of Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, In a service packed bar the two empty seats for those killed, the bereaved spoke of their lossSherelle Dresner, representing the family of Melvin Cravitz, spoke of the "lonely" and "overwhelming" new world she and her family faced in the aftermath of the attack."I have heard this new existence be described by survivors and bereaved families of other terrorist attacks as a club that no-one wants to be a part of; a club that no-one would ever choose to belong to," she said.She said she had received antisemitic abuse and "these messages should worry us all, that there are people out there justifying his murder and blaming this on his religion".Dresner praised those who "put your own lives at risk" on the day to save others, including a woman who ran "towards danger" to help Melvin.The chief rabbi, in his address to the service, said: "The attacker came here feeling positive, comfortable in his ways, encouraged and inspired by a tone of deep antisemitism within our society."We know so well how hateful thoughts can be translated into hate speech which, in turn, is only one step away from hate crime."Image source, EPAImage caption, Rabbi Daniel Walker welcomed King Charles to Heaton Park on 20 October 2025In a message read out at the start of the service, King Charles said: "My wife and I hold all those whose lives were so tragically disrupted by that terrible day most closely in our thoughts and prayers."Though the months have passed, the sense of shock and sorrow remains undiminished."The memory of those who lost their lives, Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, and of those who were injured, Andrew Franks, Bernard Agyemang and Yoni Finlay, remain especially vivid in my mind."He concluded: "Hatred can never prevail over our shared humanity."Raphi Bloom, chair of the Yom Kippur Commemoration, said the service was "not only about remembrance" but was also about resilience and "honouring Melvin and Adrian by ensuring that Jewish life continues to flourish".He said "the wounds remain, but so does our spirit" and, together, they were sending a simple message that they would not be intimidated, defined by hatred or "driven from the place we have called home for more than two centuries"."As Jews we will stand tall, united, proud and strong," he said.Image caption, Raphi Bloom was among the speakers addressing hundreds of people at Heaton Park synagogue Angela Rayner referenced other "sickening terrorist attacks" across the world when she told the congregation: "These acts are a crisis for us all - they reflect the increase we've seen in obsessive, intense hatred of Jews."She said "any attack on Jews is an attack on all of us"."Together we can overcome and defeat antisemitism – and we will never rest, until every Jewish person is safe."She said this was "a hatred we must stand robustly against, and root out from its very foundations", which meant "taking on extremists and bearing down on those who seek to divide our communities"."The only way we can root out this poison is through a whole of society approach."Image caption, Yoni Finlay said Jewish people are "having to hide their identity"Yoni Finlay, who was hit by a stray police bullet while helping to barricade the doors during the attack, said: "An evil person tried to destroy us on Yom Kippur and together we have not let that evil win."When I was lying on the floor in the foyer, just through those doors, with four of my organs badly damaged by a bullet that had gone through me, I made myself a promise, that I would not die, this is not where my life was going to end."But I could not do this on my own, and neither could the shul. We could only do this with the support of the people around us."He said he was lucky enough to have an amazing family, "but we are also an incredible community"."I realised that maybe, just maybe, we were going to be okay, when we showed that rather than being stopped, we were more together than ever".Earlier, asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about how the Jewish community in the UK feels almost a year on, he said: "I don't think things feel safer, I think we certainly live behind ever increasing gates, more security than we've ever had."Jewish people are having to hide their identity. Even my own son, who's in college at the moment, has faced death threats."Image caption, The service took place ahead of the religious anniversary, rather than following the secular calendarOther speakers at the memorial service included Alan Levy, who helped barricade the doors against the attacker, and Greater Manchester Police Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson.Although the first anniversary of the Heaton Park attack is not until October, the Jewish community will mark it on the religious anniversary rather than by the secular calendar.The attack happened on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, which falls in September this year.Rabbi Walker said the service was being held because the community also wanted to hold a public memorial before the Jewish High Holy Days, both to ensure those affected are remembered by wider society and to call for change in society.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Greater Manchester

schema.headline: Heaton Park synagogue attack memorial service attended by 800

title: Swinney says reform is at heart of his programme for government
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, John Swinney said it was "time to embrace change"ByCatherine LystBBC ScotlandThe first minister is due to set out
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, John Swinney said it was "time to embrace change"ByCatherine LystBBC ScotlandThe first minister is due to set out his plans for the year ahead which are expected to include proposals for significant public service reform.John Swinney said it was time to "embrace change", with reforms to sit at the heart of his programme for government.He has already appointed a new cabinet minister to lead on public service reform and is also expected to set out a range of policies aimed at growing the economy, eradicating child poverty, transitioning to net zero and tackling violence against women and girls.Opposition parties have said they want to see further action on the NHS and cost of living.Swinney said he was committed to making sure Scotland delivered stronger economic growth, which he said would help tackle the challenges around child poverty and investment in public services.And he said he would be setting out measures to parliament that would address "the epidemic of violence against women and girls".Eradicating child poverty Swinney is due to announce his programme for government to MSPs at the Scottish Parliament at 15:00.He said: "The government came into office with a commitment to deliver a 100-day programme, and the government is going to do exactly that."And that's the first stage of me repaying the trust that the people of Scotland have put in my government, which is to deliver what I said to the public I would deliver."He said the government had to review the way it delivered public services."We made clear before the election that was going to be necessary," he said."I want to make sure that the programme for government reflects the ambitions I set out in my election manifesto, which was all about making sure that we tackle the cost of living challenges that people face in Scotland, that we deliver improvements in our public services."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The first minister is expected to set out a range of policies aimed at growing the economyThe first minister said the government "always lives within its means"."Over the lifetime of the SNP government, we have balanced the budget on every occasion, and we will continue to do so," he said."But it also means that we've got to embrace change and change the way in which we deliver our public services."He highlighted "significant improvements" in the NHS.Swinney also said the government had made eradicating child poverty a priority and taken measures to make that possible through the delivery, for example, of the Scottish child payment and the expansion of whole family support."We work with families to help them out of poverty in addressing issues around housing or employability or, in some cases, addiction issues or childcare issues," he said."We're working alongside families to help those families get out of poverty and to make sure that children have the best chances of a start in life."It will be reinforced by the programme for government to make sure that the eradication of child poverty is written through all of the policy commitments of government to meet the expectations of the public in Scotland."The first minister said he had been "appalled" by the number of cases involving violence against women and girls over the summer months."This has been a long-running issue within Scottish society," he said."The government has taken many measures to tackle this, but I think events over the summer have said to me that I've got to exercise the strongest possible personal leadership as first minister to make sure that we tackle these issues."He said violence against women and girls could not be tolerated "in any way, shape or form in our society" and added that "making sure that we change the behaviour of men and boys in our society will be central to that programme".One of the government's proposals to tackle the cost of living issue was to introduce a price cap on some food and drink items in large supermarkets.Twenty-three organisations have since written a joint letter to Swinney urging him to scrap the plan.Signatories include groups representing retail, food and drink production, manufacturing and distribution businesses in Scotland.In response, Swinney said: "Many members of the public are struggling with the price of their shopping and I want to try to do something practical to address that and that's about bringing forward a proposal for an affordable price cap on a limited number of items within our supermarkets."We've got to consult about this and make sure the legislation can have the effect  that we want it to have and that's exactly what the government is going to do."Related topicsScotlandScottish governmentScottish ParliamentJohn
